title: Named Pipes (FIFOs) & Real‑World Pipelines 🏭
description: Create persistent inter‑process communication channels with mkfifo, and build robust data‑processing pipelines.

slides.title: What is a Named Pipe? 🎺
slides.content:
## A File That Acts Like a Pipe

A **named pipe** (FIFO) appears as a file in the filesystem, but behaves like a pipe. One process writes to it; another reads from it. Data flows in order, and reading is destructive.

Create one with: `mkfifo mypipe`.

Useful when two independent processes need to communicate.

slides.title: Basic FIFO Demo
slides.content:
Terminal 1:
```bash
mkfifo chat
tail -f chat
```
Terminal 2:
```bash
echo "Hello" > chat
```
slides.codeSnippet:
mkfifo myfifo
# Terminal 1: cat < myfifo
# Terminal 2: echo 'data' > myfifo

quizData.question: What command creates a named pipe?
quizData.explanation: `mkfifo` is the standard command; `mknod ... p` also works but is older.

slides.title: Avoiding Deadlocks 🔒
slides.content:
## A FIFO Blocks Until Both Ends Are Ready

If you open a FIFO for reading before anything writes to it, the read blocks (until something opens it for writing). Similarly, a write blocks until a reader opens.

Use background processes or separate terminals to avoid hanging. In scripts, you can use `exec` to manage file descriptors without blocking.

slides.title: Script‑Friendly FIFO
slides.content: Background a writer so the reader can start:
slides.codeSnippet:
mkfifo data_pipe
(cat /etc/passwd > data_pipe) &
head -n 3 < data_pipe
rm data_pipe

quizData.question: A named pipe can be read by multiple processes simultaneously, each getting the same data.
quizData.explanation: A FIFO is a stream; once a reader consumes data, that data is gone. Multiple readers will each get partial or interleaved data, not a copy.

slides.title: Real‑World Pipeline: Log Processor 🏭
slides.content:
## Putting It All Together

Imagine you have an API log stream. You want to:
1. Filter error lines.
2. Extract timestamps and error codes.
3. Count error types.

You can build a pipeline:
```bash
tail -f /var/log/api.log | grep ERROR | awk '{print $3, $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | tee errors.txt
```

slides.title: Live Pipeline with Process Substitution
slides.content: Feed the live count to a dashboard:
slides.codeSnippet:
mkfifo error_pipe
tail -f /var/log/api.log | grep ERROR > error_pipe &
while read line; do
  echo "$(date): $line"
done < error_pipe

slides.title: Performance Considerations ⚡
slides.content:
## Pipes Are Efficient but...

- Too many sequential pipes can slow down due to context switching.
- Use `grep -q` for early exit if you just need existence.
- Combine filters with `awk` where possible to reduce process spawning.
- For large data, consider temporary files instead of pipes (disk I/O vs. memory/CPU).

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Use `pv` (pipe viewer) to monitor throughput of a pipeline: `cat largefile | pv | gzip > out.gz`.
